rows.evidence: Q1: Material and Methods <U+2013> two-season (2007<U+2013>08, 2008<U+2013>09) replicated field experiment at BARI Gazipur with nine drip irrigation <U+00D7> mulch treatments on tomato. Q2: Results, 'Water use and water use efficiency' and Figure 1 <U+2013> at the 50% ETc level, the polythene-mulched drip plot gave the best WUE of 592 kg/ha/mm, higher than straw mulch (581) or no mulch; seasonal water use was 137, 206 and 274 mm at 50, 75 and 100% ETc.
rows.notes: The passage restates the study's own WUE result (592 kg/ha/mm = 59.2 kg/m3) for drip at 50% ETc under polyethylene mulch, so Q2 is answered yes. Caveat: all treatments were drip-irrigated; there is no furrow/surface control, so the high WUE is driven by deficit irrigation and mulch rather than by drip per se. Q3: single method (yield divided by applied water), no triangulation. Q4: the authors assert that mulch reduced soil evaporation and improved soil-water-plant relations but did not measure evaporation or soil water. Q5/Q6: one site, one soil, one crop, plot scale (4 <U+00D7> 2.4 m). Q7: the finding that mulch effect on WUE was larger at lower irrigation and that all treatments converged at 100% ETc is a variation found, not stated as a requirement. Q8: no limitations stated. Q9: CV and LSD are given for yield components in Table 2 but no dispersion measure for WUE; Figure 1 shows bars without error bars.

notes: Full text appears complete. Study is a two-year plot-scale field trial in Bangladesh comparing three drip irrigation levels with and without two mulches; no non-drip comparison treatment.
